Lesson 18 / Part 2 / ~45 minutes

Line Endings You Didn't Write

Five stages, and a file from Windows comes back the way it went in.

The buffer holds text. The file holds bytes. Whatever the file does at the end of each line is its business — the editor's job is to notice on the way in and put it back on the way out.

Every file you have opened in this editor so far was made on this machine, and on Linux a line ends with one byte: \n. Windows ends a line with two, \r\n, and most of the text files in the world were written there. Open one of those in the editor as it stands and two things go wrong at once: the cursor stops lining up with the letters, and the first line you add gets a different ending from every line around it. The second one is the bug that matters. It puts a change into the file that nobody typed, and the next git diff shows it.

By the end, the buffer holds \n and nothing else, whatever the file had; the status bar says LF or CRLF; and saving writes the file's own ending back — including on the lines you added. Three round trips are tests, and one is the experiment you run by hand in stage 1 and again in stage 5.

Before you start

You should be at the end of lesson 17: cargo test reports twenty-two passing and src/main.rs is about 770 lines. Stage 1 changes nothing and shows you the bug; stages 2 to 5 fix it, and each of the last three starts with a compiler error or a red test that you will see before you see the fix.

This lesson leans on three earlier ones. The enum Pending from lesson 15 is the model for the enum here; the match guard from lesson 5 comes back in stage 2; and the borrow rule from lesson 1 — many readers or one writer — is what stage 4's error is about.

Type it, don't paste it Same as every lesson. About a hundred lines change, half of them tests.

A file you didn't write

You have watched the editor put two kinds of line ending into a file that arrived with one.

No edits in this stage. It is an experiment, and it needs a file with Windows line endings. You don't need Windows to make one — printf will write whatever bytes you ask for:

cd editor
printf 'one\r\ntwo\r\n' > crlf.txt
file crlf.txt
→ crlf.txt: ASCII text, with CRLF line terminators
cat -A crlf.txt
→ one^M$
→ two^M$

\r is carriage return, byte 13, and \n is line feed, byte 10. The names are from teletypes, where one moved the print head back to the left and the other moved the paper up a line. Windows kept both; Unix kept the second. cat -A draws \r as ^M and the end of every line as $, so those two lines are the whole story: each line ends in both bytes. Six letters and two line breaks — ten bytes.

The character you can't see

Open it in the editor and click at the end of the first line:

cargo run -- crlf.txt
→ the status bar says 10 bytes
→ click after the e of one, or press End: the cursor sits one cell to the right of the e, with a gap between them, and the status bar says Ln 1, Col 5

Column five, on a three-letter line. The fourth character is \r. Rust gave it to egui as part of the text, because fs::read_to_string reads bytes and checks that they are UTF-8 and does nothing else. egui has no picture for it, but it still reserves a cell — measured: the same width as a letter, and no pixels in it. That is the gap. Your line_col is telling the truth about a character you cannot see.

Line numbers were right all along. ropey treats \r\n as a single line break, so char_to_line gave the right line even with the \r in the text. Only the column was off, and only by the one invisible character. Two libraries, two opinions about the same two bytes.

The line you add is different from the others

With the cursor still at the end of the first line, press Enter, type x, and save:

→ Enter, x, Ctrl+S
→ status: saved 12 bytes to crlf.txt

Then close the editor and look at the file again:

file crlf.txt
→ crlf.txt: ASCII text, with CRLF, LF line terminators
cat -A crlf.txt
→ one^M$
→ x$
→ two^M$

One line has lost its ^M. When you press Enter, egui inserts \n — one byte, the Unix ending, no matter what the surrounding text uses. Buffer::save then writes the buffer out exactly as it is. So the file now has two conventions in it, and neither file nor git diff will let that pass unremarked. (If your cursor landed on the other side of the invisible character, the bare $ is on a different line. Either way, one of the three has lost it.)

The fix is not to make egui insert \r\n. The buffer should hold one convention — \n, the one every Rust string function assumes — and the conversion belongs at the door, in open and save, where the file's bytes come in and go out. That is what the next four stages build.

Leave crlf.txt as it is Stage 3 opens it again to check the status bar, and stage 5 recreates it for the final experiment.

A name for the two endings

The editor can look at a piece of text and say which ending it uses, and four tests prove it.

This stage takes three edits: an enum, its tests, and then a repair the compiler will ask for.

First — the type. It goes between list_dir and the Pending enum from lesson 15, which it resembles:

editor/src/main.rsbetween list_dir and the Pending enum

    Ok(entries)
}

/// How a file marks the end of a line. Unix writes `\n`; Windows writes `\r\n`.
/// The buffer only ever holds `\n` — this remembers what the file had, so
/// saving can put it back.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
enum LineEnding {
    Lf,
    CrLf,
}

impl LineEnding {
    /// Which ending the text uses, judged by its first line break. Text with
    /// no line break gets `Lf`, which is what this editor writes anyway.
    fn detect(text: &str) -> Self {
        match text.split_once('\n') {
            Some((first_line, _)) if first_line.ends_with('\r') => Self::CrLf,
            _ => Self::Lf,
        }
    }

    /// The name shown in the status bar.
    fn label(self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::Lf => "LF",
            Self::CrLf => "CRLF",
        }
    }
}

/// Something the editor is waiting for permission to do.

Two variants, no data in either, the same #[derive(Clone, Copy)] as Pending. Then an impl block with two functions.

detect has no self, so it is called on the type — LineEnding::detect(text), the way Buffer::open is. It asks one question: does the first line end in \r? split_once('\n') returns an Option holding the text before the first \n and the text after it. If there is a first line and it ends in \r, the file is CrLf. The match guard — Some(…) if … — is the one from lesson 5's ErrorKind::NotFound. Everything else, including text with no line break at all, is Lf, which is what this editor would write anyway.

label takes self by value, which is fine for a Copy type, and returns &'static str. You saw 'static in lesson 8. A string literal lives inside the compiled binary for the whole run of the program, so a reference to one never has an owner that could go away, and 'static is the name for that.

What a type has to be able to do before you can test it

assert_eq! needs two things from a type. It has to compare the two sides with ==, and if they differ it has to print both, so you can see what went wrong. A type you write yourself can do neither until you say so. PartialEq is the trait behind ==; Debug is the trait behind {:?}, which you used in lesson 17's assertion message. Pending never needed either, because no test ever compared one.

derive writes the implementation for you, and for an enum with no data it is exactly what you would write by hand: two values are equal if they are the same variant, and printing one prints its name. The compiler told you the fix twice over; third — take it:

The buffer remembers what it was given

Opening crlf.txt shows CRLF in the status bar, the cursor sits against the last letter, and the column is right.

This stage takes five edits. The first three go in together and won't build until the fourth; the fifth is a test.

First — a field:

editor/src/main.rsthe Buffer struct

/// One open file.
struct Buffer {
    path: PathBuf,
    text: Text,
    /// How the file on disk ends its lines. The text above only ever holds `\n`.

    status: String,

Second — set it. Buffer::open already has the file's text in a String called text. Detect the ending from that, then replace every \r\n with \n before the rope ever sees it:

editor/src/main.rsin Buffer::open, between the match and the Self

        };
        let line_ending = LineEnding::detect(&text);
        let text = text.replace("\r\n", "\n");
        Self {
            path: PathBuf::from(path),
            text: Text::new(&text),
            line_ending,

The second new line shadows text with a new String — the same trick main uses on paths. Order matters: detect has to look at the text before replace takes the evidence away. replace builds a fresh String even when there is nothing to replace; on the 2.3 MB file from lesson 11 that is about a tenth of a millisecond, once, at open. From here on the rope holds \n and nothing else.

Writing back what you were given

A test proves that saving a CRLF file changes nothing on disk — and first, that it currently does.

This stage takes five edits: a test that fails, an import, a method, the save that uses it, and the save that compiles.

That is the whole bug in two lines, and it is why the test compares strings rather than Vec<u8>s: Debug prints a string with its escapes showing, so the \rs that are missing on the left are visible as text. Open a Windows file, save it, and it is a Unix file.

One function, two kinds of answer

Second — an import:

editor/src/main.rsthe imports at the top

use ropey::Rope;
use std::borrow::Cow;
use std::char;

Third — the method that produces what goes to disk:

editor/src/main.rsin impl LineEnding, after label

            Self::CrLf => "CRLF",
        }
    }

    /// The text as it should be written to disk. For `Lf` that is the text
    /// itself, borrowed; for `CrLf` it is a new string with every line break
    /// rewritten.
    fn apply(self, text: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> {
        match self {
            Self::Lf => Cow::Borrowed(text),
            Self::CrLf => Cow::Owned(text.replace('\n', "\r\n")),
        }
    }
}

Cow is clone on write, and it is an enum with two variants: Borrowed holds a reference, Owned holds a value. For a &str the owned form is a String. It exists for exactly this situation — a function that usually has nothing to do and can hand back what it was given, but sometimes has to build something new. The two cases have different types, &str and String, and Cow is one type that holds either.

Why not return a String every time? Because most files are Lf, and for them that would copy the entire buffer on every Ctrl+S to produce a string identical to the one you already had. With Cow, the Lf arm costs nothing — no allocation, no copy — and only the CrLf arm pays for the replace.

The '_ in Cow<'_, str> says the borrowed variant, if that is what comes back, borrows from the argument. It is the same lifetime the compiler was filling in silently for Buffer::name back when it returned &str; Cow just makes you write the placeholder.

Fourth — use it in save. The obvious way:

editor/src/main.rsin Buffer::save

        fs::write(&self.path, contents.as_bytes())?;
        self.text.mark_saved();
        self.dirty = false;
        self.status = format!("saved {} bytes to {}", self.text.len(), self.path.display());
        self.status = format!("saved {} bytes to {}", contents.len(), self.path.display());
        Ok(())

The borrow that outlived its usefulness

Read the three markers in order. contents might be Cow::Borrowed, in which case it is a borrow of self.text — line 309. mark_saved needs &mut self.text — line 311. And the borrow is still alive at line 311, because line 313 uses contents afterwards. Many readers or one writer, never both at once: lesson 1's rule, and this time the reader is a Cow.

The compiler doesn't know which variant apply returned, and it doesn't matter — a Cow that can be a borrow is treated as one. The fix is to finish with contents before mark_saved runs. Fifth — take the length first, and the borrow ends there:

editor/src/main.rsin Buffer::save, again

        fs::write(&self.path, contents.as_bytes())?;
        let written = contents.len();
        self.text.mark_saved();
        self.dirty = false;
        self.status = format!("saved {} bytes to {}", contents.len(), self.path.display());
        self.status = format!("saved {written} bytes to {}", self.path.display());
        Ok(())

cargo test
→ 28 passed
cargo run -- crlf.txt
→ Ctrl+S: saved 10 bytes to crlf.txt

Ten bytes written, eight in the status bar. The two numbers mean different things now — what is on disk and what is in the buffer — and for a Windows file they differ by one byte per line.

contents.as_bytes() works because a Cow<str> can be used wherever a &str can: it dereferences to one, the way a String does. fs::write wants bytes rather than text, and as_bytes is the same call you would make on either.

The line you typed gets the file's ending

Stage 1's experiment, repeated, leaves crlf.txt with one kind of line ending.

Stage 4 proved the untouched round trip. The bug in stage 1 needed an edit, so this stage takes two edits, both tests, and then you repeat the experiment.

First — the edit that started the lesson. When you press Enter, egui calls insert_text on your Text with a bare \n; the test makes the same call directly. insert_text belongs to the TextBuffer trait, which mod tests hasn't imported, so the call is written with the trait's full name in front:

editor/src/main.rsin mod tests, after saving_a_crlf_file_writes_it_back_unchanged

        assert_eq!(fs::read_to_string(&path).unwrap(), "one\r\ntwo\r\n");
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_line_typed_into_a_crlf_file_gets_a_crlf_ending() {
        let path = crlf_file("typed.txt");
        let mut b = Buffer::open(&path);
        egui::TextBuffer::insert_text(&mut b.text, "x\n", CharIndex(4));
        b.save().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(fs::read_to_string(&path).unwrap(), "one\r\nx\r\ntwo\r\n");
    }

Second — two tests for apply on its own, next to the ones for detect. The first checks the promise that made Cow worth using: for Lf, nothing is copied. matches! is assert!'s companion for enums — true if the value fits the pattern, and Cow::Borrowed(_) is a pattern:

editor/src/main.rsin mod tests, after the detect tests

        assert_eq!(LineEnding::detect("one\ntwo\r\n"), LineEnding::Lf);
    }

    #[test]
    fn apply_lf_borrows_the_text_as_it_is() {
        assert!(matches!(LineEnding::Lf.apply("a\nb\n"), Cow::Borrowed(_)));
    }

    #[test]
    fn apply_crlf_rewrites_every_line_break() {
        assert_eq!(LineEnding::CrLf.apply("a\nb\n"), "a\r\nb\r\n");
    }

Now the experiment. Make the file again, open it, and do exactly what you did in stage 1 — End on the first line, Enter, x, Ctrl+S:

printf 'one\r\ntwo\r\n' > crlf.txt
cargo run -- crlf.txt
→ End, Enter, x, Ctrl+S: saved 13 bytes to crlf.txt
file crlf.txt
→ crlf.txt: ASCII text, with CRLF line terminators
cat -A crlf.txt
→ one^M$
→ x^M$
→ two^M$

Thirteen bytes: three lines of one letter or three, each with a two-byte ending. The line you typed has the same ending as the two you didn't, and file has nothing to add.

What this does to a file with mixed endings detect goes by the first line break, and apply gives every line that ending. So a file that arrives with both — like the one stage 1 produced — leaves uniform after its first save. That is a change nobody typed, and it is the same kind of change this lesson set out to stop; it is smaller, it is consistent, and it is what most editors do. The honest alternative is to refuse to guess and ask — which is a dialog, and part 3's problem.

Two endings this lesson does not handle. A lone \r, which classic Mac OS used until 2001, is neither detected nor normalised. And text pasted into the editor goes into the buffer as it is — egui only normalises pasted line breaks for single-line fields — so a paste from a Windows clipboard can put a \r into a buffer that is supposed to hold none. Both are one replace away, in insert_text; neither has come up yet.

Tidy up crlf.txt is in editor/, next to scratch.md. Delete it before you commit, or it turns up in the next lesson's picker.

rm crlf.txt

Where you ended up

879 lines, thirty-one tests green. One new enum with three functions, one new field, two lines in open, three in save, two in the status bar, and nine tests. Part 2 is finished: the editor lists, navigates and opens from inside, stores filenames in the type that can hold them, and gives back the bytes it was given.

/// How a file marks the end of a line. Unix writes `\n`; Windows writes `\r\n`.
/// The buffer only ever holds `\n` — this remembers what the file had, so
/// saving can put it back.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Debug)]
enum LineEnding {
    Lf,
    CrLf,
}

impl LineEnding {
    /// Which ending the text uses, judged by its first line break. Text with
    /// no line break gets `Lf`, which is what this editor writes anyway.
    fn detect(text: &str) -> Self {
        match text.split_once('\n') {
            Some((first_line, _)) if first_line.ends_with('\r') => Self::CrLf,
            _ => Self::Lf,
        }
    }

    /// The name shown in the status bar.
    fn label(self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::Lf => "LF",
            Self::CrLf => "CRLF",
        }
    }

    /// The text as it should be written to disk. For `Lf` that is the text
    /// itself, borrowed; for `CrLf` it is a new string with every line break
    /// rewritten.
    fn apply(self, text: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> {
        match self {
            Self::Lf => Cow::Borrowed(text),
            Self::CrLf => Cow::Owned(text.replace('\n', "\r\n")),
        }
    }
}
Between these: the Pending enum, unchanged

editor/src/main.rsstruct Buffer, open and save

/// One open file.
struct Buffer {
    path: PathBuf,
    text: Text,
    /// How the file on disk ends its lines. The text above only ever holds `\n`.
    line_ending: LineEnding,
    status: String,
    /// Does this buffer hold edits that aren't on disk?
    dirty: bool,
}

impl Buffer {
    /// Open a file into a new editor. A file that doesn't exist yet is not an
    /// error — it's a new file, and starts empty.
    fn open(path: &Path) -> Self {
        let (text, status) = match fs::read_to_string(path) {
            Ok(contents) => (contents, String::new()),
            Err(error) if error.kind() == io::ErrorKind::NotFound => {
                (String::new(), format!("new file: {}", path.display()))
            }
            Err(error) => (
                String::new(),
                format!("could not open {}: {error}", path.display()),
            ),
        };
        let line_ending = LineEnding::detect(&text);
        let text = text.replace("\r\n", "\n");
        Self {
            path: PathBuf::from(path),
            text: Text::new(&text),
            line_ending,
            status,
            dirty: false,
        }
    }
    /// Write the buffer back to the file it came from.
    fn save(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
        let contents = self.line_ending.apply(self.text.as_str());
        fs::write(&self.path, contents.as_bytes())?;
        let written = contents.len();
        self.text.mark_saved();
        self.dirty = false;
        self.status = format!("saved {written} bytes to {}", self.path.display());
        Ok(())
    }
fn line_col and fn name, unchanged — 13 lines
}

Check yourself

Before this lesson, why did adding one line to a Windows file leave it with two kinds of line ending?

  • Enter inserts \n, and save wrote the buffer byte for byte
  • read_to_string dropped the \rs, and save could not restore them
  • ropey stores \r\n as one character and writes it back as \n
  • egui converts \r\n to \n when it lays the text out

Nothing was converting anything. The file's \r\ns went into the buffer and came back out; the one line you typed got egui's \n; and save wrote the mixture it was given. ↑ Review: the line you add is different from the others (stage 1)

Why does LineEnding derive PartialEq and Debug when Pending never needed to?

  • assert_eq! compares the two sides and prints them if they differ
  • An enum used as a struct field must be comparable so the struct can be
  • match on an enum needs PartialEq to test each arm
  • The status bar prints it, and printing needs Debug

The tests are the only place a LineEnding is compared or printed. match works on any enum without either trait, and the status bar prints label(), a &str, not the enum. ↑ Review: what a type has to be able to do before you can test it (stage 2)

What does returning Cow<str> from apply buy over returning String?

  • The Lf case hands back the buffer's text without copying it
  • The CrLf case can rewrite the line breaks without allocating
  • The caller can write either variant to disk without converting it to bytes
  • The compiler can check that the text is never modified after it is returned

The CrLf arm allocates either way. What Cow saves is the common case: for a Unix file, Borrowed is the same text with no work done, which a String return type could not express. ↑ Review: one function, two kinds of answer (stage 4)

Why did the first version of the new save fail to compile?

  • contents might borrow self.text, and was used after mark_saved
  • fs::write takes ownership of contents, so it was gone by the last line
  • apply takes self by value, which moved the line ending out
  • A Cow cannot be held across a call that returns a Result

The compiler can't know which variant came back, so it treats contents as a possible borrow of self.text for as long as it is used. Taking the length before mark_saved moves its last use above the mutable borrow. ↑ Review: the borrow that outlived its usefulness (stage 4)

Read this before lesson 19

Primary source: std::borrow::Cow — the type's own page. Read the opening paragraphs and the first example, which is almost exactly apply: a function that returns its input unchanged unless it has to change it. Then look down the method list for into_owned and to_mut, which are the two ways out of a Cow.

Then, if 'static and '_ are still opaque, ten minutes on chapter 10.3 of the Rust book, up to and including "Lifetime Elision". You have been using elided lifetimes since lesson 2; this is the section that names what the compiler has been filling in.

I'm your teacher here — ask me things. The status bar now shows the buffer's byte count while the save message shows the disk's. If you think the bar should show what the file would be on disk, that is either an apply on every frame or a count kept up to date on every edit — one is wasteful and the other is a cache, and lesson 8 has an opinion about caches. Ask, and we will talk it through before you pick.
